training-data.name: Training Data
training-data.bio: Podcast: Memory and Continual Learning: Engram's Dan Biderman and Jessy Lin

html_en:
The AI industry is quietly splitting into two races happening simultaneously: one for raw model intelligence, and another — arguably more consequential — for how that intelligence gets embedded into the fabric of how teams actually work.

🧠 Memory That Actually Sticks: The Case Against Context Windows

One of the more provocative ideas floating through AI research circles right now comes from Engram, a new lab founded by Dan Biderman and Jessy Lin, who appeared this week on the Training Data podcast. Their thesis: the "memory" most AI products offer today — context windows, RAG pipelines, sticky-note-style retrieval — isn't really memory at all.

"The bottleneck for making these models more useful these days is not really raw intelligence, but understanding new and evolving context... How do you bake that into the model weights the same way that pre-training and post-training bakes that into the model weights very deeply?"
— Dan Biderman, co-founder of Engram

The distinction matters enormously in practice. Externalized memory — shoving documents into a prompt — is expensive, fragile, and doesn't scale. Biderman and Lin argue that the amount of tokens individuals and teams will generate daily is approaching tens of millions, making retrieval-based approaches increasingly untenable.

"Just keeping it and searching through it is going to be pretty expensive, but it's going to also be pretty hard, pretty confusing for the models."
— Jessy Lin, co-founder of Engram

Engram's answer is continual learning baked into model weights — per-team adapter fine-tuning (LoRAs, prefix tuning, sparse architectures) trained on a company's actual documents, agent conversations, and workflows. Their partners include Notion, Microsoft, and Harvey. The payoff, they claim, could be dramatic: not having to write "monstrous system prompts" could yield "two orders of magnitude reduction in token inference consumption." Watch/Listen: Memory and Continual Learning: Engram's Dan Biderman and Jessy Lin — Training Data

🛠️ Claude Code Gets a Shareable Face

Anthropic shipped a genuinely useful feature this week: Claude Code now supports Artifacts — live, shareable web pages that are built from your coding session's full context and update themselves in real time as the agent works. Think incident timelines, PR walkthroughs, license audits, cost dashboards — all generated without wiring up data sources or standing up infrastructure.

The use case that resonates most from their internal testing is incident response: an engineer kicks off a debugging session before standup, Claude publishes a live artifact — timeline, suspect commits, error-rate chart — and by the time the team convenes, it's already been updated twice. No "walk us through what the agent found" necessary. Everyone's looking at the same page.

Artifacts are private by org by default, with role-based access controls and a compliance API for admins. Currently in beta for Claude Team and Enterprise. It's a quiet but meaningful step toward AI that produces deliverables, not just chat responses.

💰 The Applied AI Stack: Who Captures the Value?

Aaron Levie offered a sharp framework this week for thinking about where value accrues as AI costs get optimized. His argument: token cost optimization is impossible without deep, non-abstract understanding of the actual workflows being automated — which means a specialized intermediary layer between enterprises and raw model APIs is becoming essential.

"Each individual company doing this on their own is unlikely to be effective at scale, so as a consequence, this is effectively the playbook for any applied AI company right now. By evaling the models for the applied use cases, deeply understanding the domain, having tuned UX and features for the use case... enterprises get higher ROI because you actually can get more intelligence per dollar by having optimal architecture and workflows."
— @levie

This maps neatly onto the Engram thesis above: the companies that win won't just be selling access to frontier intelligence, but deeply customized, workflow-aware intelligence that costs less to run because it understands what it's doing.

📏 The Inference Budget Measurement Problem

Swyx flagged an underappreciated wrinkle in how "thinking" models get benchmarked — one that systematically disadvantages open models in published evals.

"Open models have a lot more dollar per token mileage than closed model APIs. So anyone launching an open model today or situationally incentivized toward open models should obviously report thinking levels measured by dollar inference on popular inference providers, instead of by number of tokens on the x axis."
— @swyx

If you hold inference budget (dollars) constant rather than token count, open models look considerably stronger relative to closed APIs. It's a subtle methodological point, but it matters a lot for how enterprises and researchers should interpret benchmark claims from labs — and for how open-model builders should be presenting their results.

🌱 Vibe Coding Goes Mainstream — Really

Perhaps the most striking data point of the week came not from a lab announcement but from a single tweet. @zarazhangrui noted that she's accumulated 10,000 GitHub followers over the past year — despite, by her own admission, still being unable to write code by hand.

"Last year I barely knew how GitHub worked. Now I have 10k followers on GitHub (and still can't write code by hand). What a year."
— @zarazhangrui

Meanwhile, Peter Yang shared how he built a personal health assistant called Hermes that pulls from his smart scale, Fitbit, Google Health, and a custom MCP-connected fitness app he "vibe coded" himself — delivering a weekly health digest every Saturday. It's a small but vivid illustration of what happens when the tools get good enough that the bottleneck becomes imagination rather than technical skill.

On the tooling side, @thsottiaux pushed a significant update to Codex — smoother long-thread handling, a hoverable navigation rail, better Slack Markdown paste support, and, critically, "a dedicated Pets panel." The era of AI coding tools competing on personality is apparently upon us.
html_zh:
AI工具正在悄然重塑协作方式——从代码编辑器的宠物面板到能自我更新的项目页面，今天的动态揭示了一个正在走向实用化的行业正在经历的细微但深刻的转变。

🛠️ Claude Code 的新武器：让工作成果"活"起来

Anthropic 今天悄然推出了一项颇具实用价值的功能：Claude Code 现已支持 Artifacts——将 AI 会话中的工作进度转化为可实时更新的可视化页面。

这并不是一个花哨的噱头。想象一下：工程师在早会前启动一次故障排查会话，Claude Code 自动整理日志、提交记录和错误率图表，生成一个实时页面，团队成员打开同一个链接就能看到最新进展——不需要"帮我讲讲 Agent 发现了什么"这种低效沟通。官方博客写道：

「With artifacts, team members and stakeholders don't have to 'walk us through what the agent found' because they're all looking at the same view, with the same context.」

Artifacts 支持 PR 梳理、依赖许可审计、隐私数据流图、云资源成本地图等多种场景，每次更新都发布到同一 URL，并保留版本历史。目前该功能以 Beta 形式向 Claude Team 和 Enterprise 用户开放。

🧠 AI 的"真记忆"问题：Engram 想把学习烧进权重

今天最值得深思的内容来自播客 Training Data 的一期对话。Watch/Listen: Memory and Continual Learning: Engram's Dan Biderman and Jessy Lin。

初创公司 Engram 的联合创始人提出了一个尖锐的问题：把记忆塞进上下文窗口，真的算"记忆"吗？他们的答案是否定的。Dan Biderman 解释道：

「模型今天已经非常聪明了，但我们认为让这些模型更有用的瓶颈，不再是原始智能，而是理解新的、不断演变的上下文……如何像预训练和后训练那样，把这些东西深深烙入模型权重，这正是我们研究记忆与持续学习的原因。」

Jessy Lin 则用一个生动的比喻说明了外部记忆的局限：

「就像个人写便利贴很有价值，但第二天回来上班，大脑里总有某种记忆痕迹，某种新的直觉。这两者应该结合在一起。而现在的解决方案更像是外部化记忆。」

Engram 的技术路径是：通过 LoRA 等适配器微调，针对每个团队的工作空间（合作伙伴包括 Notion、Microsoft 和 Harvey）训练专属模型，让 AI 像在公司工作多年的员工一样理解内部语境。潜在回报相当可观——Dan 提到，减少重复读取和冗长系统提示，可以带来推理 token 消耗降低两个数量级的效果。

✨ Codex 更新：宠物面板才是重点

@thsottiaux 今天发布了 Codex 的一批改进，清单相当扎实：超长对话线程流畅处理、可悬停的导航栏、设置搜索增强、Slack 粘贴保留 Markdown 格式……但他在结尾特别强调了

「And most importantly: a dedicated Pets panel.（最重要的是：专属宠物面板。）」

配套的两条推文也颇有喜感——一张图展示了"2026年操作 Codex 时的 Sol"，另一条则宣告：「跟植物说话不再奇怪了，你可以直接用 Codex。」产品的人格化，正在成为开发者工具竞争的新维度。

💡 AI 应用层的真正价值在哪里？

Box CEO Aaron Levie 今天发了一条值得收藏的长推，精准描述了当前应用层 AI 公司的核心竞争力：

「每家企业单独做这件事，规模上不大可能有效。因此，这实际上就是当下所有应用 AI 公司的打法：通过评估模型在垂直场景的表现、深刻理解领域知识、针对用例打磨 UX、以及支持落地变革……让这一层产生巨大价值。结果是企业获得更高 ROI，因为你通过最优架构和工作流，实际上可以用每一美元买到更多智能。」

与此同时，@swyx 提出了一个关于模型评测公平性的有趣视角：开源模型的推理成本普遍低于闭源 API，因此评测应以"每美元推理量"而非 token 数为横轴，这对开源模型的发布者尤为有利。

🌱 "我不会写代码，但我有 10k GitHub 星"

今天最触动人心的一条推文，来自 @zarazhangrui：

「去年我几乎不知道 GitHub 怎么用。现在我在 GitHub 上有 1 万关注者（而且我依然不会徒手写代码）。真是不可思议的一年。」

她补充说，自己并非工程师，所有项目都是出于乐趣而建，核心驱动力是"把技术和用户问题连接起来，然后讲述产品故事"。这或许是 AI 时代最具代表性的注脚之一：创造力与叙事能力，正在成为比编程更稀缺的资产。
